What happens on the first call?

We are a good fit when you want one accountable partner for strategy, build and support across web, software, automation and security.

Yes. We work with clients in Bangladesh and internationally, and run projects remotely with regular check-ins.

Can you work alongside our existing team or vendors?
Yes. We can lead a project end to end or work inside your existing team and tools.

groups.title: Scope & delivery
groups.items:
What does a typical engagement include?
Discovery, a written plan, design, build, testing, launch and handover. The exact scope depends on the service and is agreed before work starts.

How are changes handled during a project?
Changes are discussed openly, assessed for their effect on time and cost, and agreed in writing before they are made.

Can we start with one service and add more later?
Yes. Many engagements start with one priority and expand once the foundation is in place.

What do you need from us to get started?
A main contact, access to the relevant systems, and time for short reviews at each stage.

Access is limited to what the work requires, credentials are never shared in plain text, and sensitive data stays within systems you approve.

Usually, yes. We review your current tools and connect them through their APIs or through an automation platform.

posts.title: Automation for growing teams: where to start
posts.excerpt: Automate the repetitive, rule-based work first and keep people in charge of judgement. A practical way to choose your first workflows.
posts.content:
Most teams know they should automate more, but few know where to begin. The best first candidates are not the most impressive ones. They are the tasks that happen often, follow clear rules and cause real frustration when they are forgotten.

Start with a simple inventory

For one week, ask each team to note the tasks they repeat: copying details from a form into a spreadsheet, sending the same reminder, preparing the same weekly report. You will quickly see patterns.

Good first candidates

  • Routing new enquiries to the right person with all the details attached
  • Sending confirmations, reminders and follow-ups
  • Moving data between your website, CRM and finance tools
  • Producing recurring reports from data you already collect

What to keep human

Decisions that affect customers, money or reputation should stay with people. AI can draft a reply, summarise a request or suggest a category, but a person should approve anything that leaves the building.

Measure before and after

Write down how long a task takes today and how often it goes wrong. After the automation is live, check again. Clear before-and-after numbers make it easy to decide what to automate next.

posts.title: A website security checklist for growing businesses
posts.excerpt: Most website incidents start with something simple: an outdated plugin, a shared password or a missing backup. Ten checks to do this month.
posts.content:
Website security rarely fails because of sophisticated attacks. It usually fails because of small things left undone. This checklist covers the basics every organisation should have in place.

Access

  • Give every person their own login, never a shared account
  • Turn on two-factor authentication for administrators
  • Remove accounts for people who have left

Software

  • Keep the platform, themes and plugins up to date
  • Delete plugins and themes you no longer use
  • Install software only from trusted sources

Recovery

  • Take automatic daily backups stored away from the website
  • Test a restore at least once
  • Write down who to call and what to do if the site goes down

Monitoring

Set up uptime monitoring and alerts for unexpected changes. The sooner you know about a problem, the smaller it stays.

posts.title: Website or web application? How to decide what to build
posts.excerpt: A website tells people about you. An application does work for them. Knowing the difference saves budget and months of rework.
posts.content:
Many projects start with the request for "a website" when the real need is an application, or the other way round. The difference matters because they are planned, built and maintained differently.

You probably need a website if

  • The main goal is to explain what you do and generate enquiries
  • Most visitors read, compare and contact you
  • Your team needs to update pages and articles regularly

You probably need an application if

  • Users log in to do something: book, apply, order, track or report
  • The system stores records and applies business rules
  • Different people need different permissions

Often the answer is both

A common setup is a marketing website for visitors and a separate application for customers or staff, connected by a shared login or data. Planning both together avoids duplicate work and keeps the experience consistent.

posts.title: Five decisions to make before moving to a new CRM
posts.excerpt: A CRM migration succeeds or fails on decisions made before any data moves. Settle these five first.
posts.content:
Changing CRM is a good moment to fix how sales and service work, not just where the data lives. These five decisions shape everything that follows.

1. What is a lead, and when does it become a deal?

Agree the stages of your pipeline and the exact moment a record moves between them. Everything else, from reports to automations, depends on this.

2. Which data really needs to move?

Old, duplicate and incomplete records make a new system feel broken from day one. Clean and select before you migrate.

3. Which tools must connect?

List the website forms, email, phone, finance and messaging tools that should create or update records automatically.

4. Who owns the CRM?

Name a person responsible for fields, stages and user access. Without an owner, every CRM slowly fills with workarounds.

5. How will you know it worked?

Choose two or three measures, such as response time to new enquiries, and check them before and after the move.
